summary: Defines a DHCP option that gives a client its geographic coordinates, including latitude, longitude and altitude, each with a resolution indicator, plus the reference datum used. A network can use this to tell a device where it is. It was replaced by RFC 6225.

eli5.summary: When you join a network, the network can hand you a note saying where on the map you are standing. This was replaced by RFC 6225.

questions: dhcp coordinate based location configuration information
how does dhcp provide latitude and longitude
how accurate is the dhcp geoconf option
subtitle: A DHCP option for delivering geographic coordinates to clients.

tldr.problem: End devices need to know their geographic location, especially for emergency services to find users with VoIP phones, but no standard way exists to deliver this information over DHCP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3825 defines DHCP option 123, which carries latitude, longitude, and altitude with resolution indicators, plus a map datum reference. The location is stored on the end device after DHCP configuration, making it available for local use.
tldr.outcome: Devices can discover their position at configuration time and provide it to emergency responders or other applications. RFC 6225 replaced this with updated location mechanisms.

today: RFC 3825 is a Proposed Standard that has been superseded by RFC 6225, which provides updated location configuration mechanisms.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
As IP Telephony replaces traditional phone systems, users expect the same services, including automatic location detection for emergency responders. Traditional phone networks can locate emergency callers automatically, but IP Telephony typically cannot without additional mechanisms. A mobile device connected to a new Ethernet port on a campus network has no way to tell the emergency responder where it is located, and manually entering an address defeats the purpose of the technology.

This RFC proposes using DHCP to deliver geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude, and altitude) to clients at configuration time. The DHCP server determines the client's location from the circuit ID reported by the relay agent, maps that circuit ID to a physical location (such as a wall jack), and returns the coordinates. The location is then stored on the device, where the client can provide it to emergency services or applications.
sections.eli5: When you plug your phone into the network, the network tells you where that jack is. You can then tell emergency responders where to find you.

sections.title: Location Configuration Information Format
sections.content:
The Location Configuration Information (LCI) is 16 bytes long, encoded in binary for efficiency. It contains six main elements: Latitude Resolution, Latitude, Longitude Resolution, Longitude, Altitude Type (AT), Altitude Resolution, Altitude, and Datum. Latitude and Longitude are each 34-bit fixed-point numbers (9-bit integer, 25-bit fractional part), normalized to +/- 90 and +/- 180 degrees respectively. Each coordinate has a 6-bit resolution field indicating how many of the 34 bits are valid; the remaining bits may be randomized to obscure finer precision.

Altitude is a 30-bit fixed-point value whose interpretation depends on the 4-bit Altitude Type field. Two types are defined: meters (AT=1) and floors (AT=2). The 6-bit Altitude Resolution field indicates how many of the 30 bits are valid. A Datum field specifies the reference system; three are defined: WGS 84 (Datum=1), NAD83 with NAVD88 vertical datum for land (Datum=2), and NAD83 with MLLW vertical datum for water (Datum=3).
sections.eli5: The location is stored as numbers for latitude, longitude, and height. Each number has a "resolution" to say how accurate it is—a low resolution means you could be anywhere in a big area; high resolution means a tiny spot.

sections.title: Encoding and Resolution
sections.content:
The RFC provides detailed examples showing how the resolution field works. If latitude and longitude resolution are both 2 bits, the location could be anywhere in an area about 1/6 of the globe. With resolution 9 (all integer bits), it defines a 111 km × 87 km area. Resolution 18 narrows it to about 169 m × 217 m. At maximum resolution 34, the location is precise to about 3.1 mm in latitude and 2.4 mm in longitude at the equator. In emergency situations, a resolution of 20-21 bits typically yields areas around 7000 square feet, meeting North American emergency service requirements (NENA).

Altitude in meters ranges from -8388608 to +8388607 meters with 8-bit fractional precision; floors are represented similarly, with 0.0 representing ground level at the main entrance. Negative floor numbers represent basements. The resolution field allows senders to mask out low-order bits to obscure unnecessary precision while keeping the location meaningful.
sections.eli5: The resolution says how many bits of the number are true. Low resolution means the location is fuzzy; high resolution is very precise. Emergency services need about 20 bits of resolution to find a building.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Exposing geographic location information on a network creates privacy risks. DHCP messages are not encrypted by default, so an eavesdropper monitoring the link between DHCP server and client can discover the location. To minimize unintended exposure, servers SHOULD return the LCI option only when the DHCP client explicitly requests it via the parameter request list. For critical decisions based on location, DHCP authentication (RFC 3118) SHOULD be used to protect message integrity.

The resolution field does not define a privacy policy; it is purely a precision mechanism. Senders may randomize lower-order bits to reduce accuracy below the claimed resolution, but this is at the sender's discretion. Administrators deploying DHCP servers across untrusted networks must consider the potential security and privacy risks of revealing location information.
sections.eli5: Because DHCP messages travel in the clear, anyone listening on the network can see where you are. The server should only send location when you ask for it, and your network should use authentication if location is really important.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC defines DHCP option 123 for the GeoConf option. It also establishes two IANA registries: one for Altitude Type codes and one for Datum codes. The Altitude Type registry starts with Meters (code 1) and Floors (code 2); additional types require a Standards Track RFC. The Datum registry includes WGS 84, NAD83 with NAVD88, and NAD83 with MLLW, with provision for future datums that specify both horizontal and vertical reference systems.

Future extensions must be coordinated through IANA to maintain interoperability. Any new altitude type or datum must include both horizontal and vertical datum specifications when necessary.
sections.eli5: IANA maintains official lists of altitude types (meters, floors, etc.) and map datums that DHCP servers and clients should know about. New ones need official approval.
